name: Palantla Chinantec
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Palantla Chinantec is not in the catalog. The sweep list holds one work under three Glottolog records: Merrifield & Edmondson 1999 (IJAL 65(3):303-323, DOI 10.1086/466392), an instrumental study of the ballistic vs controlled stress contrast; it is closed (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar all report no OA copy; Chicago and JSTOR refuse scripted access) and only an LLBA abstract fragment was recovered via a Google Books snippet. The best first-hand placement statement was obtained instead from Merrifield 1968 Palantla Chinantec Grammar (SIL Mexico facsimile PDF, fetched sources through the Wayback Machine, scanned at 200 dpi, quotes verified against page images): one stressed syllable per phonological word, ballistic or controlled, the last toned syllable; pretonic syllables toned but unstressed, post-tonic syllables toneless and unstressed; native bisyllabic bases stressed finally; loans keep foreign stress. Rensch 1968 Proto Chinantec Phonology PDF link located but not fetched sources (Cloudflare/Wayback outage). Merrifield 1963 syllable types (Anthropological Linguistics) and the 2007 Merrifield & Anderson dictionary were not obtained. all look-ups used curl/web lookups on APIs and known sites.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word carries exactly one stressed syllable, and that syllable is the stem (the 'tonic base'): everything before it (proclitics, prefixes, pretonic bases) is toned but unstressed, everything after it (post-tonic bases) is toneless and unstressed, so the stressed syllable is always the last toned syllable of the word. Native stems are mono- or bisyllabic, and a bisyllabic native stem is stressed on its final syllable; Spanish loans keep Spanish stress. The stress itself is of two types, ballistic or controlled, lexically inherent to each base and partly alternating in verb paradigms. The language is tonal (an alternative label would be tonal-with-stress-statement).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the two 'stresses' (ballistic vs controlled) are contrasting types on the single stressed syllable, not degrees of prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-native polysyllabic bases (Spanish loans) retain their foreign stress pattern, e.g. rifey 'Efrén', kwe.to 'cuento', si.kwé.la 'escuela' (p. 19). Native bisyllabic bases are stressed on their last syllable (p. 19). Some bases show 'reverse stress' (ballistic replaced by controlled or vice versa) by person/aspect (§4.2, p. 38) - this changes stress type, not position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which may realize several grammatical words (proclitic + prefix(es) + tonic base + post-tonic base); exactly one stressed syllable per phonological word, with up to four unstressed syllables before and/or after it. The stressed syllable is the tonic base (stem): prefixes, proclitics and pretonic bases precede it (toned, unstressed), post-tonic bases (enclitic-like) follow it (toneless, unstressed) (p. 19). Palantla Chinantec is tonal; stress here is a two-way phonation-type contrast (ballistic vs controlled) on the one stressed syllable. Based on field data from San Juan Palantla, 1956-61. Data are running text and paradigms, not citation forms specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Chinantec of San Juan Palantla (municipio Valle Nacional, Oaxaca), field data 1956-61 = Palantla Chinantec, pala1351 / ISO cpa. The same variety is called Chinanteco de San Pedro Tlatepuzco / Tlatepuzco Chinantec in Merrifield & Anderson 2007 (the Palantla community descends from Tlatepuzco). Valle Nacional Chinantec (cvn, vall1253) is a distinct but related variety not covered by this source.

new_statements.reading: Culminative word stress: every phonological word has exactly one stressed syllable, which carries one of two stress types (ballistic vs controlled) and is the last tone-bearing syllable of the word; unstressed syllables (up to four) may precede it (with tone) or follow it (without tone). Stress sits on the lexical tonic base rather than at a fixed distance from a word edge; native bisyllabic bases are stressed on their final syllable and Spanish loans keep their source stress (p.19). Palantla Chinantec is therefore a tone language with lexically anchored, culminative stress that is not edge-counted; the 1999 IJAL article studies the phonetics of the ballistic/controlled contrast, not placement.
